title: ACL Injuries in Football
subtitle: From prevention to return-to-play
disclaimer: Educational content only. Not medical advice. Always consult a qualified clinician about an individual injury.

slides.title: Why ACL injuries matter
bullets: Female players have about twice the ACL injury rate of males
One of the most common season-ending injuries in football
Typical layoff of 9–12 months after reconstruction
High-profile cases: Putellas, Mead, Williamson, van Dijk

stat.label: higher ACL injury rate per exposure in female players

slides.speakerNotes: The anterior cruciate ligament, or ACL, is the main stabiliser that stops the shin bone sliding forward and twisting under the thigh bone. When it tears, a player usually loses most of a season, and often more. For every hour of football played, female players rupture it at roughly twice the rate of male players. Within about a year, the women's game lost Alexia Putellas, Vivianne Miedema, Beth Mead and Leah Williamson to this injury, and Virgil van Dijk is a well known example from the men's game. The good news is that much of this risk can be reduced.

slides.title: How the ACL tears
bullets: Most tears happen without a direct blow to the knee
Cutting, pivoting or landing on a planted foot
Knee collapses inward (dynamic valgus) with rotation
Common triggers: pressing, regaining balance after a kick, landing

stat.label: of ACL tears in professional men's football involve no direct knee contact

slides.speakerNotes: Most ACL tears happen without a direct blow to the knee. Video analysis of professional players shows that nearly nine in ten involve no direct knee contact, though many follow a push or tackle to the body. The classic picture is a player pressing an opponent, cutting sharply, or landing from a header on a planted foot. The knee collapses inward, the shin rotates, and the body is often leaning sideways. Clinicians call that inward collapse dynamic valgus. Players often describe hearing a pop, followed by rapid swelling and a feeling that the knee gives way. Because the mechanism is about movement control, it is something we can train.

slides.title: Prevention works: FIFA 11+
bullets: 20-minute warm-up: running, strength, plyometrics, balance
Use it all season, in every age group
Biggest benefit with high adherence, ideally 2+ sessions a week
Neuromuscular training roughly halves ACL injury risk

stat.label: fewer injuries overall in teams using FIFA 11+ (meta-analysis)

slides.speakerNotes: The best treatment for an ACL tear is the one you never need. FIFA eleven plus is a free, twenty minute warm-up built around running drills, strength work such as Nordic hamstring curls, jumping and landing technique, and balance. Across trials, teams using it had roughly forty percent fewer injuries overall, and neuromuscular programmes like it cut ACL injuries by about half. Adherence matters too. Teams that do it at least twice a week, as the standard warm-up all season long, get the biggest benefit. Teaching players to land softly with knees over toes is central.

slides.title: Diagnosis and treatment
bullets: Lachman test is the most sensitive clinical exam; MRI confirms
Look for associated meniscus and cartilage damage
Grafts: patellar tendon, hamstring or quadriceps tendon
Reconstruction is standard for players returning to pivoting sport
slides.speakerNotes: Diagnosis starts with the story and a careful examination. The Lachman test, where the clinician gently pulls the shin forward with the knee slightly bent, is the most sensitive bedside test. An MRI scan confirms the tear and checks for damage to the meniscus and cartilage, which is common. For footballers who want to return to cutting and pivoting, surgical reconstruction is the usual choice, using a graft from the patellar tendon, the hamstrings or the quadriceps tendon. Some less active people do well with structured rehabilitation alone, and good surgery always depends on good rehab.

slides.title: The rehab timeline
bullets: Weeks 0–2: control swelling, full extension, quad activation
Weeks 2–12: strength, balance, normal gait
Months 3–6: running, jumping, change of direction
Months 6–9+: sport-specific drills, then full training

stat.label: recommended minimum before return to matches (evidence-based)

slides.speakerNotes: Rehabilitation is a long journey, and it is driven by criteria, not just the calendar. In the first two weeks the goals are calming the swelling, getting the knee fully straight and switching the quadriceps back on. Over the next couple of months we rebuild strength and balance and restore a normal walking pattern. From around three months, if strength allows, players start straight line running, then jumping and changing direction. From six months the work becomes football specific, progressing to full team training. Returning to matches before about nine months is associated with a much higher chance of reinjury.

slides.title: Return to play and reinjury
bullets: Quad strength and hop tests ≥90% of the uninjured leg
Psychological readiness, measured with the ACL-RSI scale
Only 65% return to their pre-injury level of sport
Waiting to 9 months and passing criteria cuts reinjury sharply

stat.label: lower reinjury rate per month return is delayed, up to 9 months

slides.speakerNotes: Returning to play is a decision, not a date. We want the injured leg to reach at least ninety percent of the other leg on quadriceps strength and hop tests, along with confidence measured on a psychological readiness scale. Only about two thirds of athletes return to their previous level of sport, and young athletes face a real risk of a second ACL injury. In one landmark study, each month that return was delayed, up to nine months, cut the reinjury rate by about half, and passing return to sport criteria lowered risk dramatically. Patience and good criteria give players the best chance of a long career.
